walkthroughs.title: Growing a table with ALTER TABLE
walkthroughs.blurb: Create a table, add a column, then modify it, watching the rows.

steps.title: CREATE TABLE builds it
steps.text: CREATE TABLE member (member_id INT PRIMARY KEY, full_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, status VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'active'); then two rows are inserted, one of which leaves status out.

steps.title: DEFAULT fills the gap
steps.text: Bo's INSERT named only member_id and full_name. The column was left out, so status took its DEFAULT, 'active'.

steps.title: ADD COLUMN: existing rows get NULL
steps.text: ALTER TABLE member ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20); adds the column. The rows that already exist have no phone, so they hold NULL.

steps.title: MODIFY COLUMN restates the whole definition
steps.text: ALTER TABLE member MODIFY COLUMN full_name VARCHAR(120); widens the column, but the original NOT NULL was not repeated, so it is lost. Write VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL to keep it.

rows: MODIFY COLUMN full_name VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL

walkthroughs.title: Which constraint rejects which row
walkthroughs.blurb: Try five inserts against UNIQUE, CHECK and NOT NULL.

steps.title: The table's rules
steps.text: member(email VARCHAR(80) UNIQUE, rating INT CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5), hired DATE NOT NULL). One row already exists: ana@x.com, rating 4, 2024-01-10.

steps.title: A clean row passes all three
steps.text: ('bo@x.com', 3, '2024-02-01') is a new email, a rating inside 1 to 5 and a hire date. It is stored.

steps.title: Each rule has its own failure
steps.text: A repeated email fails UNIQUE, a rating of 9 fails CHECK, and a missing hire date fails NOT NULL. Any one failure rejects the whole row and nothing is stored.

steps.title: NULL is a special case
steps.text: A NULL rating does not fail CHECK, because the condition is unknown, not false. A second NULL email does not fail UNIQUE either. Add NOT NULL if NULL must be forbidden.

walkthroughs.title: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on one table
walkthroughs.blurb: Follow the rows of an item table through five statements, including the missing-WHERE mistake.

steps.title: Starting rows
steps.text: An item table with three rows.

steps.title: INSERT adds a row
steps.text: INSERT INTO item (item_id, name, price) VALUES (4, 'Clamp', 6.50); adds row 4.

steps.title: UPDATE with WHERE changes one row
steps.text: UPDATE item SET price = 9.99 WHERE item_id = 3; only item 3 changes.

steps.title: UPDATE without WHERE changes every row
steps.text: UPDATE item SET price = price + 1; has no WHERE, so all four rows change. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see what will be touched.

steps.title: DELETE removes rows, DROP removes the table
steps.text: DELETE FROM item WHERE item_id = 2; removes only the Saw. DELETE FROM item; with no WHERE would remove all rows but keep the empty table; DROP TABLE item; removes the table itself.

walkthroughs.title: A transfer with COMMIT and with ROLLBACK
walkthroughs.blurb: Move 100 between two accounts, then see what ROLLBACK does.

steps.title: Starting balances
steps.text: Account 1 holds 500 and account 2 holds 200. Total: 700.

steps.title: START TRANSACTION, then subtract
steps.text: START TRANSACTION; UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 1; Inside the transaction the total is now 600: 100 is missing until the second update runs.

steps.title: Add to the other account
steps.text: UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE account_id = 2; The total is back to 700.

steps.title: COMMIT makes it permanent
steps.text: COMMIT; Both changes are saved together and other users now see them. A ROLLBACK after this cannot undo them.

steps.title: The failure case: ROLLBACK
steps.text: Suppose the second UPDATE had failed. Run ROLLBACK; instead of COMMIT. The subtraction is undone and the balances return to 500 and 200, so no money is lost.

walkthroughs.title: How an index finds a row
walkthroughs.blurb: Compare a table scan with a lookup through a sorted index.

steps.title: Without an index: read every row
steps.text: WHERE email = 'kim@x.com' on a table of 48,000 rows with no index on email: MySQL must read the rows one by one until it has checked them all.

steps.title: CREATE INDEX builds a sorted structure
steps.text: CREATE INDEX idx_member_email ON member (email); builds a BTREE: a sorted tree of email values, each pointing at its row.

steps.title: A lookup walks the tree
steps.text: The search compares at each level and drops down one branch: root, branch, leaf, then the row. Three or four steps instead of 48,000. Ranges and ORDER BY work too because the values are sorted.

steps.title: The price: slower writes
steps.text: Every INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE must also update the index, and the index takes storage. DROP INDEX idx_member_email ON member; removes it if nobody uses it.

rows: Write the row and update the index

walkthroughs.title: Reading EXPLAIN before and after an index
walkthroughs.blurb: Spot a full table scan, add an index, and check that EXPLAIN now uses it.

steps.title: EXPLAIN shows the plan, not the rows
steps.text: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM member WHERE email = 'kim@x.com'; returns one row describing how MySQL would run the query.

steps.title: Read it: a full table scan
steps.text: type = ALL means every row is read, key = NULL means no index is used and rows = 48000 is the number examined. This is the sign an index may help.

steps.title: Add an index and EXPLAIN again
steps.text: CREATE INDEX idx_member_email ON member (email); then the same EXPLAIN gives type = ref, key = idx_member_email and rows = 1.

steps.title: A function on the column hides the index
steps.text: WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2024 cannot use an index on order_date, because the function is applied to every value. The rewrite order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-01-01' can. LIKE 'Ok%' uses an index but LIKE '%kafor' does not.

walkthroughs.title: Who waits when two users update
walkthroughs.blurb: Compare table-level and row-level locks, then watch a deadlock form.

steps.title: Two users, two different rows
steps.text: User A updates seat 5 and user B updates seat 9 in the same table at the same moment.

steps.title: Table-level lock: B waits
steps.text: With a table lock, A holds the whole table, so B must wait even though the rows differ. Simple, but low concurrency.

steps.title: Row-level lock: both run
steps.text: With row locks (InnoDB), A locks only row 5 and B locks only row 9, so both run at once. Finer locks give more concurrency at the cost of tracking many locks. Field-level, a single value, is the finest grain in concept.

steps.title: Same row: shared and exclusive
steps.text: Many users can hold a shared (read) lock on a row together. An exclusive (write) lock is held by one user and blocks readers and other writers until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

steps.title: Deadlock
steps.text: A locks row 5 and then wants row 9. B locks row 9 and then wants row 5. Each waits for the other, so neither can continue. InnoDB detects this and rolls one transaction back so the other can finish.
